teaser_de: Teil 3 der Serie Season Stats 2025: die Defense der 49ers in Advanced Stats.
teaser_en: Part 3 of the Season Stats 2025 series: the 49ers defense in advanced stats.
body_en:
*Season Stats 2025, part 3 of 4. The series by Chris Pracher: Part 1: Understanding advanced stats · Part 2: Season Stats 2025, offense deep dive · **Part 3: Season Stats 2025, defense deep dive** · Part 4: All advanced stats at a glance.*

## A bottom-8 defense: the 49ers' 2025 defense, analyzed without mercy

As exciting as the 49ers' offense was in 2025, the look at the other side of the ball is just as unsparing, because the advanced stats find hardly anything good to say about this defense. Anyone looking for a real strength at team level will find practically none: in almost every relevant category, this defense ranked in the bottom eighth of the league. The only number that looks even respectable turns out, on closer inspection, to be average at best, and even that one is flattering. So the crucial question is not whether this defense was bad, but how much of it reflects real substance and how much was the result of a wave of injuries that hit the most important players of all.

Key finding: bottom 8 of the league in almost every category (DVOA 27, EPA 26, success rate 29). The only passable number, EPA against the run (10), is average at best and even flattering: against efficient runs, the defense was bottom 4 at rank 29.

## The big picture: bottom 8 wherever you look

Let's start with the bird's-eye view, because it shows the full extent of the misery. Defensive DVOA was +9.0 percent, which meant rank 27, and on defense a positive value is bad, of course: the unit allowed about nine percent more than an average defense. Nor is this a fluke of a single metric, because EPA/play of +0.077 (rank 26) and a success rate of 48.2 percent (rank 29) paint exactly the same picture. Ranks 26, 27, 29: that is not merely below average, that is the bottom eighth of the entire league.

But wasn't there at least a bright spot against the run? At first glance, yes, because EPA/play against the run of -0.089 meant rank 10. This number does not deserve praise, though, but a sober assessment. First, rank 10 out of 32 is average at best and certainly not a strength. Second, and more importantly, the number is flattering: EPA punishes explosive big plays above all, and the Niners prevented those reasonably well. But the actual down-to-down defense against the run was dismal, as the rushing success rate of 45.3 percent (rank 29) shows. On the ground, opponents stayed on schedule almost at will and only missed out on the really big runs. Viewed soberly, the run defense was mediocre at best, too.

And the rest, the pass defense? A disaster. Against the pass, EPA was +0.179 (rank 27) and the success rate 50.0 percent (rank 26). Putting it all together, there is simply nothing to sugarcoat about this defense at team level: a single number in the middle of the pack, everything else in the league's basement.

## The pass rush: a Bosa-shaped hole

Why the pass defense collapsed can be traced in large part to a single absence. Nick Bosa, the engine of the entire pass rush, tore his ACL at the end of September and missed practically the whole season, and without him there was hardly any consistent pressure. Pass rush win rate, which measures how often a defender beats his blocker within 2.5 seconds, exposes the gap mercilessly: among the edge rushers, only Yetur Gross-Matos reached a halfway usable value at 16.3 percent (rank 18), while Bryce Huff was mediocre at best at 14.3 percent (rank 35). Behind them, though, there was a chasm: the badly injured rookie Mykel Williams (8.8 percent, rank 95) and the young interior tackles Alfred Collins (4.7 percent, rank 102) and C.J. West all lagged far behind.

Pass rush productivity, which combines sacks, hits and hurries, confirms the picture: the best 49ers value here came from Huff (6.8, rank 67), which already shows that not a single rusher on the front came anywhere near a league-leading level. A tactical detail from the FTN almanac underlines the predicament: the defense's average box count fell from 6.28 (rank 4) in 2024 to 6.00 (rank 31) in 2025, so the 49ers pulled more personnel back into coverage and still got run over through the air. When even a defensive base concept focused on pass defense doesn't help, the pressure up front is simply missing.

## The linebackers: Warner as the rock, thin air behind him

At the center of the defense stood, as in every healthy year, Fred Warner, at least as long as he was healthy. His missed tackle rate of 7.7 percent (rank 20) confirms his usual reliability, and in coverage he was clearly respected at 8.2 coverage snaps per target (rank 31), with an allowed reception rate of 72.7 percent (rank 14), which is presentable for an off-ball linebacker in a zone scheme. But Warner, too, ended up missing time, and behind him the air got thin: Dee Winters (missed tackle rate 13.1 percent, rank 56) and Tatum Bethune (16.0 percent, rank 74) had to take on more responsibility than was good for them and clearly allowed too much in coverage, with reception rates above 80 percent. Warner thus remained largely a soloist in a unit that, without his ideal partner Dre Greenlaw, supported him only inadequately.

## The secondary: one bright spot, a lot of basement

The only truly positive surprise of the entire defense came from the secondary, and it has a name hardly anyone would have expected before the season: Renardo Green. The cornerback allowed a reception rate of just 52.1 percent (rank 14), less than almost any other defender on the roster, and combined that with an outstanding missed tackle rate of only 4.5 percent (rank 7), making him the most reliable player in the entire back seven. In a difficult season, Green was the rock in the storm. But in all honesty, one strong cornerback does not turn a rank-27 defense into a good one.

Because around him, things got thin quickly. Cornerbacks Deommodore Lenoir and Darrell Luter were respected with high coverage-snaps-per-target values of 9.4 and 9.6 (ranks 9 and 7), meaning quarterbacks tended to avoid their side, but when they were targeted, both allowed too many catches with reception rates around 65 percent. And among the young safeties, the real lack of substance became apparent: Ji'Ayir Brown delivered a usable value with a reception rate of 62.5 percent (rank 19), while Malik Mustapha and rookie Marques Sigle showed with high reception rates and weak forced-incompletion numbers (Mustapha 3 percent, rank 89) how much work remains to be done here. The secondary was young, thin and left on its own for long stretches, because the pass rush gave it no help whatsoever.

## Conclusion: a major construction site, not a repair job

In the end, the uncomfortable question remains: is this bottom-8 defense a structural defect or just a snapshot of the infirmary? An honest answer takes both seriously without downplaying the weakness. Yes, the loss of Nick Bosa and the periods without Fred Warner explain a considerable part of the collapse, above all the nonexistent pass rush. But the numbers were not just bad, they were almost consistently in the bottom eighth of the league, and that cannot be explained away by injuries alone. A young secondary that was overwhelmed for long stretches and a front that, apart from the injured Bosa, had not a single real pass-rush weapon are also a talent and depth problem.

Naive optimism for 2026 is therefore out of place. A healthy Nick Bosa should noticeably lift the pass defense, if only because his pressure gives the whole secondary room to breathe, but it is a long way from rank 27 even to the middle of the pack, and whether a young group under new defensive coordinator Raheem Morris can make that jump is anything but certain. The names Bosa, Warner and Green at least form a framework. But measured against what the 2025 advanced stats show, this defense is not a case for fine-tuning with one or two adjustments, but a genuine major construction site. Anything else would be sugarcoating.

Go Niners!
